parts:
Dear Adrian,
dear all,

the ChangeLog of QCA 3.7 says:

"o Improved: new method of deriving the intermediate solution, without
      using any counterfactuals. This restricts the intermediate solution
      to only one model for each combination of conservative and parsimonious
      models"

What does this exactly mean? I am just analysing a minimizing output and the same procedure leads to different intermediate solutions with QCA 3.6 and 3.7.. Additonally the intermediate solution with 3.7 seems odd, because some conditions/combinations from the conservative and parsimonious solution do not appear anymore.

Is this explainable?

Thank you and best regards

Max

messages.subject: Re: [QCA] new method for deriving the intermediate solution in 3.7
parts:
Thanks Max, but I meant a reproducible example.
Something I can get my hands on to study in depth, and search why the intermediate solution looks the way it looks.

But generally speaking, nothing changed in terms of applying the directional expectations. That is still exactly the same procedure described by Ragin and Sonnett in 2005, the only thing that did changed was how to obtain the final (intermediate) solution after the dialogue between the conservative and parsimonious models.

What I found in that presentation is that sometimes, due to employing the easy counterfactuals, we get <more> than one intermediate model for each pair of CS and PS models. Which is weird, because (and Charles Ragin confirmed it) there should be one and only one intermediate model for each such pair. More than one model is a by-product of the easy counterfactuals method, and it happens that one of those models is identical with the one I get using the new method (Quine expansion) and the rest of the models simply stray away from the complexity - parsimony continuum.

Now, if we care about this continuum, no model that strays away should be reported (otherwise we need to revisit that continuum and I don't believe this leads anywhere). And it so happens that one and only one model is certainly found on the continuum, and no others (at least I was unable to find any other similar intermediate models).

That is the only difference. The model reported by QCA v 3.7 should definitely have been reported by the easy counterfactuals method. On the other hand, the easy counterfactuals method (sometimes) reports more models that do not obey the continuum.

I am more than sure your example has a logical explanation, but I have to get my hands on the example to dig deeper. The algorithm behind it is automatic, and if passed all my tests so far (although I would be happy to stand corrected, this will only improve the method and make it more robust).

Best,
Adrian

Dear Adrian,
dear all,

actually I wanted to avoid uploading my dataset publicly, but perhaps the example is valuable for the community and the development of the package. Enclosed you will find the dataset to work with and here is the code I used:

ttGROW <- truthTable(data=Setdata, outcome = "GROW",

                      conditions = "FINBIG, SUBS, FFF, PERS, BUSINESS, EO",

                     incl.cut=0.79, n.cut = 2, sort.by="incl, n", complete=TRUE, show.cases=TRUE, dcc=TRUE)

 

# conservative solution

 

csGROW <- minimize(ttGROW, details=TRUE, show.cases=TRUE, row.dom=TRUE, all.sol=TRUE)

 

#parsimonious solution

 

psGROW <- minimize(ttGROW, include="?", details=TRUE, show.cases=TRUE, row.dom=TRUE, all.sol=TRUE, use.tilde=FALSE, neg.out = TRUE)

 

 

#intermediate solution

 

isGROW <- minimize(ttGROW, include = "?", details=TRUE, show.cases=TRUE, row.dom=TRUE, all.sol=TRUE,

dir.exp = "FINBIG, FFF, SUBS, FINBIG*SUBS, FINBIG*FFF,FFF*SUBS,                    PERS, BUSINESS, EO, BUSINESS*EO")


I hope this helps to explain the differences in the intermediate solutions with 3.6 and 3.7. (Please ignore the fact that the data seem not to be "really" fuzzy. That is a point which I want to discuss in another treat.)

Bests,
Max

OK Max, I'll have a look.

To avoid having to upload your actual data, the best method is to produce the simplest possible (real or fabricated) dataset for which the observed behavior still persists. This involves either randomly create a small dataset, or subset your actual data to the maximum extent possible, and eventually change the column names or obfuscate it in such a way that it would be unusable for anything else but for the replication process itself.

I do understand you have observed the behavior on your actual data, and to test the behavior on a fabricated mimimal data would involve running two separate versions (3.6 and 3.7) of the QCA package. This is not very complicated either, the procedure I am using is to create a temporary directory, and install the version I want to compare against there, something like:

dir.create("TEMP")

install.packages("path/to/QCA_3.6.tar.gz", lib = "TEMP", quiet = TRUE, repos = NULL)

Thanks Max, but I meant a reproducible example. 
Something I can get my hands on to study in depth, and search why the intermediate solution looks the way it looks. 

But generally speaking, nothing changed in terms of applying the directional expectations. parts: And I should have also mentioned something about your directional expectations:
"FINBIG, FFF, SUBS, FINBIG*SUBS, FINBIG*FFF, FFF*SUBS, PERS, BUSINESS, EO, BUSINESS*EO"

Here, FINBIG*SUBS is redundant since FINBIG is there too. Same with the conjunction BUSINESS*EO, since both BUSINESS and EO are atomically present. In fact, the whole expression is logically equivalent to:

simplify("FINBIG, FFF, SUBS, FINBIG*SUBS, FINBIG*FFF, FFF*SUBS, PERS, BUSINESS, EO, BUSINESS*EO")

# S1: BUSINESS + EO + FFF + FINBIG + PERS + SUBS

Which is pretty much equivalent to a statement that all conditions lead to producing the outcome when present. There is no added value in the rest of the expression.

Best,
Adrian

What I found in that presentation is that sometimes, due to employing the easy counterfactuals, we get <more> than one intermediate model for each pair of CS and PS models. Which is weird, because (and Charles Ragin confirmed it) there should be one and only one intermediate model for each such pair. More than one model is a by-product of the easy counterfactuals method, and it happens that one of those models is identical with the one I get using the new method (Quine expansion) and the rest of the models simply stray away from the complexity - parsimony continuum.

Hi again, Max and all,

Upon studying this example for other combinations of CS and PS models, I realised that even with the new method there can be multiple concurrent intermediate models. This happens because a sufficiently large SOP expression can have multiple equivalent simpler versions.

The lesson I learned is that, with or without the easy counterfactuals, it might not always be possible to restrict the intermediate solution to only one model for each combination of CS and PS models.

Dear Adrian,

thank you for this deep analysis. I am glad that the example was useful!

I also deleted the neg.out, which seemed to be a transmission error. Your comments concerning the combinded directional expectations are also very helpful. Thank you.

For me, one question arises from this example with 20 parsimonious and 21 conservative solutions: How much ambiguity do we want to allow and how could we (or should we) avoid ambiguity? Further: How should we treat model ambiguity? I think this is a topic that needs further discussion in the literature, as our models will become more complex. To have only one intermediate solution for each combination is a good first step, I guess. But in my case it would still mean 20x21 solutions.

Best,
Max
Am Samstag, 28. März 2020 12:51:08 UTC+1 schrieb Adrian Dușa:

Hi again, Max and all,

Upon studying this example for other combinations of CS and PS models, I realised that even with the new method there can be multiple concurrent intermediate models. This happens because a sufficiently large SOP expression can have multiple equivalent simpler versions.

The lesson I learned is that, with or without the easy counterfactuals, it might not always be possible to restrict the intermediate solution to only one model for each combination of CS and PS models.

However, I suspect some models might still deviate from the complexity / parsimony continuum, so instead of mechanically applying the new method I might look for a way to verify which models do, and which models do not obey the continuum. It remains to be seen what to do next, because something like this has not been done before.

Thanks again Max for the example, very useful indeed,
Adrian

Dear Max,

The thing is, and credit to your example, I realised that it is not always possible to have only one intermediate model. For instance this expression:

> simplify("C~D + ~CD + ~B~C + ~B~D")

S1: ~B~C + ~CD + C~D
S2: ~B~D + ~CD + C~D

It has two, equally valid, equivalent simpler solutions. Which means it is always possible to have model ambiguity within the intermediate solution(s), where I was previously convinced the is (or should be) no ambiguity at all.

Given that model ambiguity is bound to exist, it doesn't really matter if the resulting models are minimal or not. Then your use of argument all.sol = TRUE should yield the same models as those in version 3.6. I made a modification in the development version, and starting with the upcoming (patch) version 3.8 you will notice the reversion to the previous interpretation in 3.6 allowing maximal model ambiguity.

But there is another side of your question, I guess. Since there are 20 models in the CS and 21 in the PS, you will have at least 20x21 different IS solutions. This is not model ambiguity though, these are solutions. Each solution can have one or more models, and only in the latter case you can have ambiguity. Some IS solutions might have a single model with no ambiguity at all.

There is no way to restrict the number of CS models or the number of PS models. I might perhaps filter out some of the IS models, by verifying if they are found in the complexity / parsimony continuum, but you will always end up with that as models for the CS and PS.

In the fs/QCA software, users are required to decrease (or even eliminate) ambiguity by choosing specific prime implicants from the resulting PI chart. The R package automatically calculates all possible combinations and users can decide post-factum on which specific combination to focus. But the flip-side of the coin is to generate a lot of solutions, each potentially presenting model ambiguity.

What to do with a high model ambiguity might be a different topic: perhaps focus on the essential prime implicants, or chose those models with highest coverage etc.

Best,
Adrian

Further: How should we treat model ambiguity? I think this is a topic that needs further discussion in the literature, as our models will become more complex. To have only one intermediate solution for each combination is a good first step, I guess. But in my case it would still mean 20x21 solutions.
